segments.text: Welcome to your daily Robotics digest for October 27, 2026.
We've got updates on Optimus charging, world model predictions, and massive robot supply chain moves.
Tune in now.
From Humanoids Daily, Tesla’s Lars Moravy floats Optimus as a Cybercab charging helper.
This story concerns a proposal suggesting that the Optimus robot could assist with charging Cybercab vehicles by interacting with existing charging infrastructure.
Lars Moravy's proposal focuses on Optimus bridging the gap in physical interaction required for connecting to established charging systems.
The discussion indicated that this proposed role involves physical interaction with built infrastructure rather than fully automating the entire charging process.
Details regarding Optimus's battery size and production status were also mentioned in the report.
This development suggests exploration into how advanced robotics can interface with existing physical systems for utility functions.
Further developments in physical interaction technology will be closely observed by the industry.

From Humanoids Daily, WorldOracle tests whether world models can reliably predict real-world executions, and the evaluation found discrepancies between predicted and actual object states during manipulation tasks.

The benchmark assesses action-conditioned world models by comparing their predictions against actual robot executions, focusing on the accuracy of predicting object positions and movements during manipulation.

The methodology involved testing model performance across various time horizons, observing that while arm motion prediction often demonstrated good accuracy, object states frequently deviated from reality.
Prediction errors were quantified using metrics such as Physical State Correctness and Interaction Spatial Alignment to measure alignment with real outcomes.
Developers can contribute by submitting predictions from open-weight or closed-source models for iterative refinement.
This research indicates that current world models exhibit limitations in fully capturing the complex dynamics of physical interactions over extended operational sequences.
Future work will focus on improving the fidelity of state estimation in embodied AI systems.
From Humanoids Daily, Boston Dynamics tapped Korean suppliers for Atlas, with 10,000-robot preparations reported.
This report details the supply chain strategy employed by Boston Dynamics to procure components for its humanoid robot development.
Hyundai Mobis is positioned as a central supplier, providing most actuators and collaborating with Korean battery and camera manufacturers.
The reported supplier selection prioritizes cost control and reducing dependence on Chinese components.
This supply chain effort leverages Hyundai's automotive manufacturing experience for Atlas production.
Final quantities and pricing remain undecided, with initial orders potentially appearing in late 2027 or early 2028.
This development indicates a strategic shift in the hardware sourcing for advanced humanoid robotics.
From The Guardian - Artificial Intelligence, "‘Autonomy, not flesh’: RAF chief outlines AI drone-powered future".
This report details the Royal Air Force chief's vision for an autonomous, drone-powered future in warfare, emphasizing the reduction of direct human involvement.
The chief advocates for integrating artificial intelligence into military operations, proposing that Typhoon fighters will operate alongside four AI drones designed for long-range patrolling.
This technological shift is intended to move military roles towards the outside and alleviate recruitment pressures.

These unmanned systems will function as a force multiplier by positioning sensors and weaponry within contested airspace, supporting the Royal Air Force's objective to be ready to fight against Russia by 2030.
The development signals a focus on autonomous systems integration within defense technology sectors.
From Robotics & Automation News, Omron to acquire US industrial computer maker OnLogic for $675 million.
This report details Omron's acquisition of OnLogic and its parent company Interlogic, a transaction valued at six hundred seventy-five million dollars.
The acquisition is intended to advance Omron's industrial automation business into the areas of manufacturing digitalization and physical artificial intelligence.
OnLogic designs configurable industrial computers specifically for applications involving automation, edge artificial intelligence, and the Internet of Things.

The transaction is scheduled to finalize around January of twenty twenty seven, with plans for Omron to integrate OnLogic's hardware with existing technologies to develop novel data and artificial intelligence intensive industrial solutions.
This move signals an expansion of industrial technology integration within the automation sector.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Comau integrates Nvidia technology to accelerate development of AI-powered robots".
This report details Comau's integration of Nvidia technologies to advance the development of AI-powered robotics and automation for industrial use.
The collaboration involves powering industrial robot controllers with Nvidia Jetson edge compute and integrating the robot portfolio into Nvidia Isaac Sim for simulation and testing.
Furthermore, Comau is utilizing the Nvidia software stack to optimize vision features and control strategies for intralogistics products.
This effort encompasses training artificial intelligence models through reinforcement learning for tasks such as palletizing and depalletizing within these simulated environments.
This methodology aims to accelerate the deployment of smarter, more autonomous robotic solutions in real-world industrial settings.
This development signals a trend toward leveraging advanced computing platforms for tangible industrial automation deployment.
From Robotics & Automation News, Qualcomm to acquire PickNik to expand open-source robotics and physical AI capabilities.
This report details the agreement for Qualcomm to acquire the robotics software company PickNik to enhance its open-source robotics and physical artificial intelligence capabilities.
The acquisition is designed to streamline the transition for developers moving from artificial intelligence models to operational robotics systems.

The integration will involve incorporating the open-source motion planning framework MoveIt, which will retain its open-source status with community involvement, alongside PickNik's commercial platform.

This combined technology will be integrated with Qualcomm's Dragonwing robotics platforms and Arduino boards to establish a connection between AI models and motion planning for advanced robotic applications.
This development signals a convergence between foundational AI and physical motion control systems in robotics.
From Robotics & Automation News, Bedrock Robotics raises six hundred million dollars to scale autonomous excavators across the United States.
This financing supports the expansion of autonomous machine deployment on commercial construction sites.
The funding, co-led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital, is allocated to expanding the deployment of autonomous excavators.
The company has already demonstrated fully autonomous excavators successfully performing paid work on live job sites.

Bedrock Robotics is concentrating on establishing the necessary field, commercial, and operational infrastructure required to establish autonomy as a dependable component of the construction industry.
The new capital will facilitate expanded deployments, strengthen field operations, and enhance partnerships for integrating intelligent systems into construction projects.
This development indicates a growing focus on integrating autonomous hardware into heavy industry applications.
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: How much RTK fix do your outdoor robots keep under tree canopy? Field data and a test design"
investigates the quality of RTK fix performance for outdoor robots operating under tree canopies.
A field test compared receiver performance under open sky, under trees with rain, and under trees with network RTK corrections.
In long-baseline sessions, most receivers achieved one hundred percent fix status, although some dropped to eighty-three point three or eighty-eight point five percent fixed under tree conditions.

The study notes that fixed flags do not necessarily prove accuracy due to varying conditions and a lack of ground truth, and it recommends a specific test design for evaluating receivers in tree environments.
This research provides necessary guidance for developing robust positioning systems in complex outdoor settings.
From Humanoids Daily, Boston Dynamics Employee Petition Against ICE Robot Deal Tests Its Ethical Guardrails reports on a dispute concerning a pending deal for modified Spot robots with U.S.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the employee petition against the transaction.
Boston Dynamics management confirmed the sale while emphasizing existing restrictions against weaponization and harm to people.

The dispute arises from concerns raised by employees regarding the extent of responsibility physical AI makers possess concerning customer applications and acceptable uses, suggesting the association with ICE could negatively affect the company's reputation and recruitment efforts.

This situation illustrates the difficulty physical artificial intelligence companies face in establishing comprehensive deployment guidelines beyond basic safety considerations for customer applications.
The matter indicates a need for further industry-wide standards regarding the deployment of physical AI systems.
From Robotics & Automation News, Edeka adds Knapp robots to automate meat picking at a German distribution center.
This report details the integration of two Knapp Pick-it-Easy robots to automate the picking of fresh meat products with high efficiency.

The expanded logistics operation at the Nordfrische distribution center now incorporates these AI-powered robots which operate continuously to autonomously recognize and handle various fresh meat products.
The system is capable of achieving around four hundred fifty picks per robot per hour while simultaneously scanning barcodes and recording weights to ensure process quality.
This automation leverages Knapp's KiSoft software for intelligent control across the entire logistics sequence, enhancing supply chain resilience and reducing strenuous tasks for personnel.
This development demonstrates the increasing application of advanced robotics in complex food distribution environments.
From Humanoid.guide, GXO expands Agility Digit deployment to two more US warehouses.
This report details the expansion of the Agility Digit deployment to new facilities in North Carolina and Tennessee, commencing installations in early 2027.
GXO Logistics is expanding its Agility Digit deployment to two additional warehouses in North Carolina and Tennessee, with installations scheduled to begin in early 2027.
The initial deployment will utilize Digit 4 for e-commerce fulfillment, with a subsequent plan to adopt Digit 5 as it becomes commercially available.
This expansion builds upon a pilot program that was initiated at the Flowery Branch, Georgia facility.
The deployment demonstrates customer value, despite GXO noting a lack of return on investment for humanoid robots.
GXO will proceed with Digit 4 and plan to migrate to the newer Digit 5 upon its commercial availability.
This movement indicates continued industrial adoption of advanced digitization solutions within the logistics sector.
From Robotics & Automation News, Canada’s Charl-Pol creates robotics joint venture with Norway’s Storvik.

This report details the formation of Alumotion, a joint venture focused on applying automation and robotics to Canadian aluminum smelters to enhance operational efficiency and address workforce safety.
The collaboration merges Charl-Pol's specific local smelter knowledge with Norway's established European automation expertise.
Alumotion will concentrate on deploying robotics for the manual task of anode assembly repair, a process currently executed by human labor.
This partnership facilitates the integration of advanced robotics into heavy industry operations by leveraging specialized international knowledge.
This alliance signifies an expansion of international technological collaborations within the aluminum sector.
Future developments in industrial robotics are expected to reflect increased cross-border technological integration.
From The Robot Report, Xpanner launches autonomous pile driver for solar farm construction.
This report details the introduction of the X1 Piling R6, an automated robot designed for the autonomous installation of posts for utility-scale solar and battery energy storage sites.
The system utilizes high-precision GNSS and onboard sensors to guarantee accurate pile placement, overseen by a single operator.
The robot is powered by a ninety-seven kilowatt engine and a hydraulic hammer capable of driving piles up to twenty-three feet in length.
Project teams have the option to use Xpanner Connect to manage installation schedules and monitor the installation data remotely.
The operational model involves a mixed capital expenditure and software as a service subscription, with Xpanner managing the initial setup and support phases.
This development signifies advancements in robotics application for heavy civil construction sectors.
Further developments in autonomous infrastructure deployment are anticipated.
From The Guardian - Artificial Intelligence, "Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll".
This report details the impact of the intensifying competition for artificial intelligence supremacy between China and the United States on Chinese financial markets, resulting in significant losses.
Heavy government investment in artificial intelligence has not translated into profitability for many technology companies due to weak domestic consumer demand.
The focus within China is currently directed toward embodied artificial intelligence and robotics, yet consumer demand for these specific products remains low.
Concerns are being raised regarding the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom given these economic and geopolitical pressures.
This situation signals potential shifts in technological focus and market stability within the global technology sector.
From Humanoids Daily, "Tesla’s Optimus Gen 3, Figure 04 and the Next Apollo: When Each Could Be Revealed".
This report details the projected timelines for the unveiling of next-generation humanoid robots from various development groups.
Figure is developing Optimus Gen 3, focusing on human-like hands and simplified manufacturing, with a likely reveal slated for late 2026 or early 2027.
Tesla is currently engaged in the internal construction of Optimus Gen 3 robots, with anticipated customer deliveries potentially occurring toward the end of 2027.
Concurrently, Aptronik is advancing work on its next Apollo successor, with an estimated reveal set for 2027.

Other prominent humanoid developers include Boston Dynamics with Atlas, Agility Robotics with Digit 5, and 1X with NEO, none of which have publicly established firm reveal dates for their subsequent models.
These developments indicate an ongoing race among entities to advance humanoid robotics capabilities in the near future.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Orbbec Gemini 330 series: Active stereo cameras built on proprietary MX6800 ASIC depth processing".
This report details the development of active stereo cameras utilizing proprietary hardware for internal depth and color alignment.
The Orbbec Gemini 330 series cameras employ the proprietary MX6800 ASIC to compute depth and internally align it with color information by operating active and passive stereo simultaneously.
This integrated in-camera hardware manages both depth generation and the necessary depth-to-color alignment, which reduces the computational demands on the host systems.
The family includes models such as the Gemini 335 for compact configurations and the Gemini 335L designed for applications demanding extended range and increased accuracy.
This architecture provides robotics and automation sectors with integrated, robust, and low-latency depth sensing capabilities.
The advancement points toward more efficient and sophisticated perception systems in automated environments.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, StarBot Nova!".

This report details the introduction of StarBot Nova, a wheeled service humanoid developed by StarBot USA for restaurant, hospitality, and retail environments, demonstrating its capabilities in mobile sorting tasks.
StarBot Nova measures one hundred fifty-two centimeters tall and weighs thirty-two kilograms, utilizing a differential drive base and two articulated arms for locomotion and manipulation.
The robot operates at a speed of four point three kilometers per hour and possesses a strength rating of five kilograms, with a battery life of ten hours per charge.
Confirmed capabilities include obstacle avoidance and the sorting of goods achieved through the integration of Intel RealSense and RGB cameras.
The unit is currently a prototype with a published price of twenty thousand United States dollars, establishing it as an early platform for commercial mobile sorting applications.
This development signals further advancement in the deployment of mobile robotics within commercial service sectors.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, ZWHAND A17!".

This segment reports on the specifications and rating of the ZWHAND A17, a compact robotic hand manufactured by Shenzhen ZWHAND Technology Co., Ltd., which achieved a Humanoid.Guide Hand Score of six out of ten.
The ZWHAND A17 is a robotic hand measuring two hundred forty-four millimeters in length and weighing zero point eight five kilograms, closely mimicking human hand proportions.
The assessment indicates a higher dexterity score of four out of five compared to its strength score of two out of five, highlighting a focus on fine motor control capabilities.
This model is priced at five thousand US dollars and falls within the manufacturer's product family range between the B06 and B20 models.
The development of such articulated, dexterous components indicates ongoing advancement in the field of advanced robotics and human-machine interaction design.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, MagicBot Gen1!".
This report details the introduction of the MagicBot Gen1, a humanoid robot developed in Wuxi, China, demonstrating capabilities in research, manufacturing, and service.
The robot measures one hundred seventy-four centimeters tall and weighs seventy kilograms, featuring bipedal locomotion and articulated arms.

It is equipped with an eight-core CPU and a one hundred TOPS AI processor for onboard computing, utilizing LiDAR and depth vision for obstacle avoidance during tasks such as sorting goods and product assembly.
The system supports connectivity via 5G and WiFi 6, and is currently listed as in production with a price point of fifty thousand US dollars.
The robot's skill score is categorized in the developing stage, indicating a focus on structured trials for current autonomy levels.
This development signals ongoing progress in physical robotics integration within industrial applications.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, 4NE1 Gen 4!".
This report details the introduction of the 4NE1 Gen 4 humanoid robot, a development resulting in enhanced physical work capabilities.
The robot measures one hundred eighty centimeters in height and weighs sixty-five kilograms and was developed by NEURA Robotics in Germany for physical tasks alongside humans.
It possesses fifty-five degrees of freedom and features advancements in the fourth generation, including lighter textile skin and more precise hands.
The robot is capable of performing tasks such as sorting goods, assembling products, and managing household chores like folding clothes and emptying a dishwasher.
It employs onboard NEURON AI processing with multi-sensory feedback for interaction and navigation, incorporating obstacle avoidance.
The unit is currently in production with a listed price of seventy thousand United States dollars, highlighting integrated industrial and household manipulation.
This progression indicates continued development in the integration of advanced AI with physical robotics for domestic and industrial applications.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, ZWHAND B20!".
This segment reports on the specifications and performance assessment of the ZWHAND B20 robotic hand.
The device received a Humanoid.Guide Hand Score of six out of ten, indicating a capable or mature performance level.
The rating breakdown reveals a Degrees of Freedom rating of four out of five, which is stronger than its Strength rating of two out of five, suggesting a focus on dexterity over gripping force.
The ZWHAND B20 is currently in production, costs six thousand five hundred United States dollars, weighs zero point six kilograms, and is manufactured in China.
This data reflects current advancements in robotic manipulation technology and sets a benchmark for dexterity in manufactured end effectors.
From Humanoid.guide, Welcome, Linker Hand L30 Pro!
This segment reports on the evaluation of the Linker Hand L30 Pro robotic hand, which received a Humanoid.Guide Hand Score of seven out of ten.
The evaluation profile specifically emphasized dexterity, achieving a perfect five out of five for Degrees of Freedom, while the Strength rating was two out of five.
This result indicates a design prioritizing movement versatility over raw gripping force.
LINKERBOT has listed the L30 Pro as currently in production, with pricing details available upon inquiry.
The assessment suggests that potential purchasers should weigh the importance of dexterity against gripping force for specific operational applications.
This data contributes to the ongoing evaluation of robotic hand capabilities in the current technological landscape.
And that’s all the circuits for today!
Hope your day is as smoothly powered as Optimus floating around.
Thanks for tuning into the Robotics Digest.
See you tomorrow!
